1.pericope_label: O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you? This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh? Have ye suffered so many things in vain? if it be yet in vain. He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you, doeth he it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?

schools.summary: Work the two reproaches lexically: trace the verb for bewitching to its sense of bringing evil by feigned praise or the evil eye, with the papyri supplying the adjective for unharmed by it, and separate the milder word for foolish, used on the walk to Emmaus, from the sharper one elsewhere, so that it names an undisciplined reasoning faculty in a people intellectually shallow; then find the irony in the tenses of begun and finishing, concede that the single question of verse two settles the matter, and recover the Athenian chorus-word behind ministering.

Refuse to let the reproach become a national one, since it points neither to any Galatian reputation nor to the unregeneracy common to all men but to their present stupidity about justification, it being egregious folly to leave Christ for Moses; and hear the passage as passion rather than method, an expostulation inserted amid the doctrine because the rejection of the Son of God would rouse any pious mind to indignation, the apostle's word for them meaning disordered in mind.

Press the practical questions the argument turns on: whether this one argument might not convince them by itself, and what exactly they are said to have suffered — since the verb serves as readily for possessing and enjoying as for losing, so that the question may be whether they have received and lost so much good rather than whether they were persecuted; and keep the chorus-image concrete, of leading up the chorus and adding grace to grace, benefit to benefit.

Head off the superstition the word invites: the glance of the eye has no natural power to injure and the organ itself cannot be evil, since to behold is simply its function while to behold in an evil manner belongs to a mind depraved within — the term standing for jealousy, which wealth and pomp generate because they are perceived through that sense.

Defend the apparent disorder of the letter as design rather than defect: Paul intermingles gentle exhortation with sharp reproof by his own rule to Timothy, to be instant in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke and exhort, so that the simple reader who thinks he keeps no order is measuring by the rhetoricians when the order that governs him is spiritual.

Make the folly culpable rather than merely intellectual, since it is not enough to know the truth and say we believe it — we must obey it too, and those are spiritually bewitched who will not obey truth plainly set before them.

sides.position: Persecution, probably at the hands of their own Jewish countrymen, whose rage they had braved for the gospel
Not necessarily persecution at all: the verb serves for possessing and enjoying as well as for losing, so the question may be whether they had received and lost so much good
Persecution, though there is no record of any in North Galatia and there is for the south

debates.question: Who is it that ministers the Spirit and works miracles?

sides.position: Paul himself, which is said to be the common opinion of all the ancient commentators
God, which the obvious reference requires

outliers.note: Alone treats the evil eye as a physical claim needing refutation, arguing that the organ cannot be evil since to behold is simply its function, and that what the term names is jealousy, generated by wealth and pomp because these are perceived through the eye.

Alone defends the letter’s abruptness as method, holding that Paul observes no order by the rhetoricians’ measure but a goodly order as concerning the spirit, on his own rule to Timothy to reprove, rebuke and exhort.

6.pericope_label: Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Know ye therefore that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham. And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed. So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.

schools.summary: Argue the case from chronology and from grammar: the most eminent of the patriarchs was justified before the law of Moses was given, so the law cannot be necessary to justification; the personification that makes the Scripture foresee falls in with a standing Jewish formula about what the Scripture saw; the compound verb for preaching the gospel beforehand occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; and the quotation draws its all the nations from the later promise rather than the all the tribes of the earlier.

Defend the choice of witness, since arguments from examples are not always conclusive but this one admits no exception in either subject or person, there being no variety of roads to righteousness; explain why the instance bites, Abraham being the first of the circumcision and the head of the nation the false teachers gloried in; and let the preposition carry the weight at the close, not with Abraham as circumcised or as a Hebrew but with the Abraham who by faith alone obtained a blessing that means adoption into eternal life.

Bring the rabbinic admission into court, that the Jews themselves held Abraham could obtain an inheritance neither in this world nor the world to come but by faith; and observe that the same argument is still live, since from Abraham the Jews draw their case both for continuing in Judaism and for denying the Gentiles to be the church of God.

Rename what is under discussion and the dispute changes shape: the promise is a testament, and a testament is not a law but a donation, since heirs look for no burdens laid upon them but for the inheritance confirmed; then split the patriarch in two, a working Abraham and a believing Abraham, and disclaim all interest in the first.

Call the promise to Abraham a preaching of the gospel to him, and infer from it that true believers of whatever nation are blessed with him and in the same manner as he was, by faith in the promise and not otherwise.

debates.question: Why does Paul say seed and not seeds?

sides.position: Because the promise, by its very wording, pointed to the Messiah, who is the descendant of Abraham above all others
Because Abraham had two seeds in his house, one natural in his own household and one spiritual in those like him by faith
It is a rabbinical refinement, though an intelligible one: the word is a collective which Paul himself applies to all believers, and he does not claim Christ is specifically meant in the Genesis text

outliers.note: Alone sets Paul beside James on the same verse of Genesis and judges that the two are discussing different episodes in Abraham’s life and that both are correct.
Alone produces the rabbinic admission that Abraham could obtain an inheritance neither in this world nor in the world to come but by faith.

10.pericope_label: For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them. But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith. And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them. Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree: That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

schools.summary: Picture the curse as a blade hanging overhead and trace the word to its parts, then note that the quotation is the close of the curses pronounced on Ebal, slightly altered so that it speaks of things written in the book; complete the picture from the prepositions, since we were under a curse and Christ became a curse over us, standing between us and what was overhanging; observe that the verb for redeeming is not the usual word for ransom but the general word for buying up; and find force in an abrupt opening without any connecting particle.

Be exact about who is threatened, since Paul says neither those who were under the law nor those who do its works — the works of the law are to be done, only not for righteousness, and it is the not doing that entails the curse; argue the rest from contradictories, the same fountain not yielding both hot and cold, while guarding that the law is not contrary to faith in itself but only in the matter of justification; and insist that Paul does not say Christ was cursed but the stronger thing, that he was made a curse.

Turn the quotation into a textual case: no printed copy of the Hebrew preserves the word answering to the apostle's all, and Jerome reports that it was suppressed lest men appear bound to perform everything written in the law, though the reading stands in manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, in the Samaritan text, in the Targum and in the Septuagint; then state the law's demand as a change of question, since it asks not what a man believes but what he has done, and requires perfect, uninterrupted and perpetual obedience.

Spend the anger on the expositors rather than the text: Jerome and the schoolmen who follow him, seeming with a godly zeal to turn the reproach of the curse away from Christ, said that Paul did not speak in earnest and that Moses meant only a hanged malefactor — which is to make the Scripture disagree with itself in order to spare it.

debates.question: Should the Hebrew of the quoted curse read all?

sides.position: Yes, though no printed copy of the Hebrew Bible preserves it: it stands in manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, in the Samaritan text, in the Targum and in the Septuagint, and Jerome reports that the Jews suppressed it
The apostle's Greek quotes it, and he modifies the Septuagint only to read of things written in the book rather than of words

debates.question: Is the law contrary to faith?

sides.position: Not in itself, or God would be unlike himself; the contradiction lies only in the matter of justification, where one may sooner unite fire and water
In its whole demand, since it asks not what a man believes but what he has done

outliers.note: Alone turns the quotation into a textual case, tracing the missing Hebrew word for all through Jerome’s charge of suppression and the manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, the Samaritan text, the Targum and the Septuagint.
Alone builds the doctrine out of the prepositions, so that we were under the curse, Christ became a curse over us, and the buying out is a movement from under to out.

themes: the just shall live by faith

15.pericope_label: Brethren, I speak after the manner of men; Though it be but a man’s covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto. Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect. For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise: but God gave it to Abraham by promise.

schools.summary: Supply the legal vocabulary the illustration runs on, the word serving for both covenant and will, the participle for ratifying standing in a perfect passive of completed and authoritative confirmation, and the verb for adding to it found nowhere else; then handle the interval and the text critically, noting that the figure is the Exodus date for the sojourn in Egypt which the Greek version enlarges to take in the patriarchs' years in Canaan, that the oldest manuscripts omit the phrase confirming the covenant in Christ, and that contract and free gift are incompatible ideas.

Hear the address soften from foolish Galatians to brethren, the blame imputed rather to their teachers; take the illustration as meant to put them to the blush, since it is base that the testimony of God should weigh less with us than a mortal man's, the argument running from the less to the greater without levelling the distance between them; and block the narrower escape at the close, that only ceremonies are in question, when what is weighed is the justifying effect attributed to them and the obligation laid on the conscience.

Give the illustration in the forms of the present day, an agreement signed, sealed and witnessed, standing under the protection of the civil law so that nothing may be erased or added, and not even the covenanter himself may disannul it; then distinguish the two arguments being made, the first drawn from the time of the transaction and the second from its nature.

Say openly that the argument looks weak, since in weighty matters we ought to confirm earthly things by divine and not the reverse, which is the way of the schoolmen; then state the Jewish objection at full strength before answering it, that God, mistrusting his own promises as insufficient to justify, added something better four hundred and thirty years later, so that the law abrogated the promise.

Mark the difference the covenant makes to the form of a promise: the promises of the law are made to the person of every man, while the promises of the gospel are made first to Christ and then through him to those ingrafted into him by faith.

debates.question: Is the phrase confirmed of God in Christ genuine?

sides.position: No: the oldest manuscripts omit it and it should certainly be struck out
It stands, and refers to the promise of justification made to believers in Christ

debates.question: Is the illustration from a human covenant a fit argument?

sides.position: It is weak on its face, since in weighty matters we ought to confirm earthly things by divine and not the reverse
It runs from the less to the greater and puts them to the blush, without placing God on a level with men

outliers.note: Alone judges the apostle’s own argument weak on its face, holding that heavenly matters ought not to be confirmed by earthly ones, which is the manner of the schoolmen.
Alone strikes words from the received text at this verse, since the oldest manuscripts omit the phrase that makes the covenant confirmed in Christ.

themes: not to seeds but to seed

19.pericope_label: Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; and it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one. Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid: for if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law. But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.

schools.summary: Answer the question about the law's purpose from the word added, which makes it no part of the original scheme but a marginal addition and a parenthesis in the design of providence, the direct line running through promise and fulfilment; allow the phrase because of transgressions to cover both checking them and multiplying them; deny any contradiction, since the law is a thing apart that in no way modifies the covenant's provisions; register the scale of the mediator crux, counted at three hundred interpretations by one estimate and over four hundred by another; and draw out the shutting up as a net, a lid or a fold.

Put the objection in the objector's mouth first, that there had as good been no law at all, and then refuse to let the mediator verse be made metaphysical: some philosophize about the twofold nature of Christ, but no man of sound judgment doubts that the contracting parties are meant, and the real question, which the common exposition leaves undetermined, is why the statement was introduced — perhaps to anticipate a wicked thought that God retracts his covenants as men do.

Keep the law's use concrete as a straight edge laid against crooked conduct, given that we might know our sinfulness and our need of mercy; divide the question by dividing the law, since the ceremonial yoke was probably inflicted as punishment for the national sin of idolatry and lasted only till Christ, while the moral law was added to discover and restrain transgression and does not pass away; and settle the mediator by counting parties, God being only one of them and Abraham not present in the days of Moses.

Describe what the law does to a man rather than what it is for: when sin, death, wrath and judgment are revealed to him he cannot but grow impatient, murmur against God and despise his will, since he can neither bear the sentence nor escape it — and the man who out of temptation was very holy, bowing his knee and giving thanks like the Pharisee, now falls into hatred of God.

Hold the purpose steady against the objection: the law was not designed to disannul the promise, nor to establish a different way of justification from the one the promise had settled, but was added for ends that serve it.

debates.question: What does it mean that the law was added because of transgressions?

sides.position: To check or put down transgressions
To multiply and increase them, as in Romans
The expression is wide enough to cover both senses
To make sinfulness known, the law being a straight edge that shows the crookedness of conduct

debates.question: What does it mean that a mediator is not a mediator of one?

sides.position: No passage in the New Testament has exercised so much learning to so little purpose, and it seems to defy every attempt at a satisfactory sense
Moses is not the mediator of that one seed to whom the promise was given
The contracting parties are meant, and the statement anticipates a wicked thought that God retracts his covenants as men do
There must be two parties or there is no mediator, and God who made the free promise was only one of them
The count of proposed interpretations runs to three hundred or four hundred and thirty
Over four hundred interpretations have been made

outliers.note: Alone describes the law’s effect on a man rather than its purpose in the design, so that the holy man out of temptation, who bowed his knee and gave thanks like the Pharisee, falls into hatred of God when the sentence is revealed to him.

Alone asks why the statement about the mediator was introduced at all, faulting the common exposition for leaving the question undetermined, and suggests it anticipates the thought that God retracts his covenants as men do.

23.pericope_label: But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed. Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.

schools.summary: Render the custody exactly — kept in ward, the Law a prison-house and a stern guardian from which escape was not permitted — and find in the imperfect tense a long progressive imprisonment rather than a single act; then correct the word schoolmaster at length, since the office belonged to a slave or freedman whose main duty was not instruction but watching over boys from about six to sixteen and conducting them to the schools, his care ceasing where the schoolmaster's began though it was he who chiefly formed the character, as Horace noted when his own father took the part.

Guard the opening clause against a false inference, since faith coming does not mean the grace of faith was absent before, the Old Testament saints having the same Spirit and the same faith as to nature, object and use; note that the words to bring us are a supplement with nothing answering them in the original; and date the change by the veil of the temple rent in two, concluding that under Christ's reign no childhood remains that needs a schoolmaster, while at once asking again whether the law is so abolished that we have nothing to do with it.

Draw the verse into the argument about the canon, that the God of the two Testaments is one, who foretold in the older the Christ who appeared in the newer, and who by the Law and the Prophets led us to Christ's school — the tutor clause serving as proof that the two dispensations have a single author.

Press the comparison where it hurts: a schoolmaster is profitable and necessary, yet show me one scholar who loves his master, and what love the Jews bore Moses appears from their readiness at any hour to stone him — so it is not possible that the scholar should love the man set over him, and the law's office is felt as tyranny until faith is revealed.

State plainly what the office could and could not do: the law taught no living, saving knowledge, but by its rites and above all its sacrifices it pointed to Christ, as children are led to school by the servants who have the care of them, and the gospel state is by so much the greater advantage.

Keep the figure of the household servant rather than the teacher, the man who led the children to school and brought them back and had charge of them out of school hours, so that the law taught no saving knowledge but by its rites and sacrifices directed us elsewhere; and observe that as the Law names the whole Mosaic economy, so the Faith names the whole of the gospel and not merely the act of believing.

sides.position: Not the grace of faith, which the Old Testament saints had in the same nature, object and use, but the doctrine of faith, never before so clearly preached
The faith in Christ as Saviour, made possible by his historic coming, as the definite article shows
The dispensation of faith which was in store, for which the guardianship was fitting us

outliers.note: Alone turns the schoolmaster into an argument about affection, asking to be shown one scholar who loves his master and citing the readiness of the Jews to stone Moses at any hour.
Alone generalises the two articles, that as the Law names the whole Mosaic economy so the Faith names the whole of the gospel and not merely the act of believing.

26.pericope_label: For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.

schools.summary: Object to the word children, since the point is that the Christian is no longer a child but a grown son, the age before the Messiah standing to the age after it as minority to full age; guard sonship against a national sense, Jesus having called the Jews sons of the kingdom in privilege though not in fact; take the clothing metaphor as a badge or uniform of service and as the putting on of another's sentiments and traits; and prefer there is not to there cannot be, a statement of fact rather than possibility, the pairs dividing the human race exhaustively.

Sort out the ways sonship might be meant and keep only adoption, neither by nature as Christ is nor by creation as Adam and the angels; add that it would not be enough to say we are no longer children unless we are also freemen, since in a slave age alters nothing; make the garment mean a union so close that they bear Christ's name and character before God and are viewed in him rather than in themselves; and name what the last verse is for, not to rank descent from Abraham above membership in Christ but to repress the pride of those who reckoned no distinction higher.

Note that the apostle always has by faith, in faith, of faith in his mouth, and never says they are children of God because they are circumcised; divide the putting on of Christ into one according to the law, which is to follow his example, his singular patience and inestimable mildness, and another according to the gospel; then lengthen the list of abolished stations — neither magistrate nor subject, teacher nor hearer, master nor servant — while guarding that these are the good creatures of God and are nothing only in the matter of salvation.

Keep the profession in view: in baptism we put on Christ and therein profess to be his disciples, being baptized into his death, that as he died and rose again we should die unto sin and walk in newness of life.

Draw the obligation out of the metaphor, since to put on a man is to assume his person and character and whoever does so is bound to act his part; and document the disparity the third pair cancels from Jewish practice, where a man might shave his head and rend his clothes in mourning and a woman was not permitted, and a man might impose the vow of the nazirite on his son where a woman could not on her daughter.

debates.question: Is there or can there be neither Jew nor Greek?

sides.position: There is not: a statement of fact rather than of possibility, against the reading that makes it a bare impossibility
There cannot be

debates.question: What is it to put on Christ?

sides.position: To take him to oneself, in the ordinary sense of the Greek Old Testament, the white baptismal robes being only a suggested source for the figure
To put on his sentiments, opinions and characteristic traits as a man clothes himself, which was common language among ancient writers
To assume his person and character, and so to be bound to act his part
Two things at once: according to the law, to follow his example and virtues; according to the gospel, something else
To be so closely united to him as to bear his name and character before God, and be viewed in him rather than in ourselves

outliers.note: Alone documents the disparity that the third pair cancels, from the Jewish rules on mourning, where a man might shave his head and rend his clothes and a woman might not, and on the vow of the nazirite.

Alone extends the abolished distinctions beyond the apostle’s three to magistrate and subject, teacher and hearer, master and servant, and then guards them as the good creatures of God, nothing only in the matter of salvation.
